items.title: ‘Take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego? Trump is beyond irresponsible | Ted Widmer
items.summary: We appear to be entering a new era, in which political desperation at home leads to increasingly unhinged threats abroad Donald Trump was in Nebraska on Monday, and though his long rally speech had elements of a performance, this was no Bruce Springsteen album. He offered another dark meditation on a world spiraling out of control, one in which the destruction of American cities is increasingly a possibility, unless Americans trust him to use the vast powers of the presidency to annihilate his foes. The president drew fury when he suggested that Iran could launch a nuclear attack and “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego. California leaders reacted with scorn at Trump’s alarmism. Iran says Hormuz Strait to remain closed until US meets seven conditions
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz Strait to remain closed until US meets seven conditions Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has said that the Strait of Hormuz will remain shut until Washington meets certain conditions. Ghalibaf, who also acts as Tehran's chief negotiator in the talks, said that the contested waterway will remain closed until seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding are met by Washington. He conceded that the US had made "some proposals through a mediator" after Tehran presented a seven-day roadmap to reopen the strait. But he warned Washington that "the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over" and Iran's position remains "clear and definite".

items.title: California leaders condemn Trump’s remarks about possible attacks on US cities
items.summary: California leaders condemn Trump’s remarks about possible attacks on US cities California political leaders on Tuesday condemned President Donald Trump after he said Iran could “take out” US cities including Los Angeles and San Diego, describing the remarks as dangerous and unacceptable. Speaking at a political rally on Monday, Trump was discussing the economic costs of war when he said: “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego.” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said Trump’s remarks could compromise the city’s safety, while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said: “We are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” California Governor Gavin Newsom also criticised Trump, calling him “deranged”. Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president, adding that “no American city is expendable and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity." Vance also indicated that the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. "We're not going to trade words for actions," he said.

Last month, Iraq enforced the US ban on Iranian carriers, especially at Najaf’s airport, which is a major hub for Iranian flights. items.title: Lessons from the Iran War
items.summary: The Iran war offers broader lessons about the limits of force, the resilience of revolutionary regimes, and the unpredictability of modern conflict. Military action can weaken an adversary without producing decisive political outcomes, while economic pressure, alliances, energy markets, and public opinion can prove equally consequential. The conflict also exposed vulnerabilities in alliance coordination, munitions stocks, counter-drone capabilities, and strategic communication. Effective deterrence ultimately requires hard power, resilient partnerships, clear objectives, and the political will to sustain them.

items.summary: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating. It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. De politie vreesde dat er explosieven in de witte busjes lagen en woningen werden uit voorzorg ontruimd. Er werden enkel blikken benzine in de busjes gevonden. Op diezelfde dag werden er vijf Britse mannen aangehouden. Later bleek dat een van de verdachten eerder al zelf de politie had gebeld . Op 1 oktober werd nog een verdachte opgepakt. De zes verdachten zijn allemaal in de twintig. Ze mogen verder onderzoek op vrije voeten afwachten. items.title: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions'
items.summary: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions' The US and nine other countries across the Americas in a joint statement condemned what they called Iran's "terrorist actions". The joint statement was released by the US and endorsed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago. "On 5 October, the undersigned nations, condemn the terrorist actions and other malign influence operations in our hemisphere by Iran and its terrorist proxies," it read. "These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security." The joint statement indicated that the countries "stand united" against "such threats", demanding that Tehran and "its proxies must halt these actions now".

items.title: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran
items.summary: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran The chief executive of Saudi Aramco warned that the world's oil stockpiles are now "scarily thin". In his first public speech since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Amin Nasser said the conflict reduced oil supply from the region by "nearly 3bn barrels", with over 1bn barrels of oil released from reserves to cushion the depletion. Nasser estimated that "less than 6bn barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available". "The system is already straining," he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."

clusters.headline: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis

items.title: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis
items.summary: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could lead to a global food security crisis, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), John Denton, warned. According to the Wall Street Journal, Denton indicated that if the vital waterway is not reopened, grain prices could rise by up to 80 percent. The situation in the strait has also caused a shortage of around 2.7 million tons of fertiliser on the world market, a decrease of nearly 40 percent. Such obstacles could affect international agricultural production and food supplies, making import-dependent countries especially vulnerable. The report noted that the ICC is working with the UN and the International Maritime Organization on a mechanism that would transfer temporary management of navigation through the waterway to the UN secretary general. However, the ongoing tensions between the US and Iran have hindered its implementation, the report added.

clusters.headline: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind

items.title: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind
items.summary: On September 30, the U.S. completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq. Heralding this event, Iraq declared “Sovereignty Day,” celebrating the end of U.S. occupation and return of full sovereignty to the people of Iraq. In practice, this withdrawal was little more than the departure of a few hundred soldiers that had returned to Iraq in 2014 – at the invitation of the Iraqi government – to provide support and assistance to the collapsing Iraqi Army in its fight against ISIS. Unlike the hundreds of thousands of troops needed in Germany and Japan at the end of WWII, the troops of Operation Inherent Resolve were neither an occupation nor a challenge to sovereign control. Nonetheless, the mission had become a political liability and a convenient excuse for anti-government militias to maintain independence, retain weapons and force its will both in the streets and within Parliament. While some voices in Washington argue for a keeping residual military presence , the reasonable solution is shifting to a diplomatic and development effort. This was U.S. policy after the first withdrawal

items.summary: Houthis target Riyadh airpot, declare Saudi airspace open target except for holy sites The Iran-affiliated Yemeni group targeted King Khaled International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh for the second time on Monday. "In response to the Saudi aggression against our country in the past 24 hours ... the Yemeni armed forces targeted King Khaled Airport in Riyadh," the military spokesperson said in a statement. The statement said the strike was precise and disrupted air traffic at the airport. The strike comes after the Houthis issued an earlier warning on Monday against using Saudi airspace. "The Saudi skies are open theatre for our operations, except for the holy airspaces of Makkah and Madinah," the Houthi warning said. "We disclaim all liability for the consequences of ignoring our warnings against continuing to use the Saudi airspace," it added.

The Peshmerga are Kurdish armed forces, with roots going back to Kurdish guerrillas who fought as a more or less united front against successive Iraqi governments for most of the 20th century. After the 2003 invasion, though, they never came together as one Kurdish national army. Instead, they split into two separate party forces, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), each tied to one of the region's dominant political factions. items.summary: The current war with Iran and its chaotic unfolding open a door of great danger for the U.S. and the planet. At best, we are condemned to negotiations dominated by personal and political imperatives that seem to fit with a common description of insanity — to keep doing the same thing and expect a different result. At worst, the crisis raises the prospect that tactical nuclear weapons could be employed to solve it. The situation has now become so grave, and its implications for the global economy so devastating, that even China — which otherwise is notoriously disciplined in avoiding entanglement in other countries’ conflicts — has indicated openness to joining a mediation effort to end the conflict. Both China and the U.S. are right to be concerned about the crisis. The two have a mutual interest in solving this problem and keeping it from becoming a worse irritant. items.title: Three commercial vessels struck in Hormuz since 1 Oct, UKMTO says
items.summary: Three commercial vessels struck in Hormuz since 1 Oct, UKMTO says Attacks on commercial ships witnessed a surge during the past three days, as at least three tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) warnings. Early Saturday, UKMTO reported that a crude oil tanker was hit on its port side approximately 4 nautical miles east of Oman. A day earlier, an outbound vessel suffered a small fire and blackout, while a second crude tanker was struck nearby. On Thursday, a supertanker carrying 2.5 million barrels caught fire after being hit off Oman while transiting an unauthorised route, according to Iran's Fars news agency. In its weekly Voluntary Reporting Area Overview released on 2 October, UKMTO said 91 incidents of damage to vessels have been reported since February this year. Three tankers have been struck in and around the Strait of Hormuz since 1 October 2026. (AFP)

items.title: Iran's warns 'half-a-century-old' UAE over claim on three Gulf islands
items.summary: Iran's warns 'half-a-century-old' UAE over claim on three Gulf islands Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, has warned the United Arab Emirates (UAE) against challenging Tehran and its sovereignty over three islands in the Persian Gulf. In a post on his X account, Velayati dismissed recent claims made by the UAE at the United Nations General Assembly regarding sovereignty over Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, and Abu Musa, saying the three islands will remain Iranian forever, according to IRNA. "A country whose political life does not reach half a century makes claims from the UN podium about islands that have been recorded under Iran's name in historical documents and maps of past centuries," Velayati said in the Farsi-language post. He added that the UAE should not "rely on foreign powers" for its security and should instead pursue good relations with its neighbours, IRNA reported. "The neighbour stays, and the guest goes… Regional experience has shown that imported security has an expiration date," said the former Iranian foreign minister.

Benjamin Netanyahu ha dicho que correrá la misma suerte que los abatidos líderes de Hamás, Yahya Sinwar, y de Hizbolá, Hasán Nasrala. Es Abdul Malik al Houthi, el líder del movimiento rebelde de Yemen, los hutíes, que desde hace más de diez años controlan la capital, Saná, y, cada vez más, el paso estratégico de Bab el Mandab, que une el Mar Rojo con el océano Índico.Abdul Malik al Houthi no estaba llamado a dirigir el movimiento político-militar de la minoría chií de Yemen. En cierto modo, su llegada al poder fue similar a la del cachorro de los Assad de Siria –también perteneciente a una minoría chií– Bashar al Assad , que pretendía ser dentista, pero la muerte de su hermano mayor le impuso el deber de ser líder de la dinastía. items.summary: De copiloot die woensdag zijn gezagvoerder aanviel in een vliegtuig van Flydubai werd eerder geschorst bij vliegmaatschappij Oman Air. De man werd destijds als een risico voor de veiligheid gezien omdat er extremistisch materiaal bij hem was aangetroffen. Dat zeggen bronnen tegen het Amerikaanse nieuwsmedium ABC News . Deze bronnen zijn hoge functionarissen van inlichtingendiensten en de rechtshandhaving, meldt ABC. Zij zeggen dat de man in 2024 werd betrapt op het bezit van extremistisch materiaal, toen hij als copiloot in opleiding werkte voor Oman Air. Volgens de bronnen mocht hij na de schorsing wel in een administratieve functie blijven werken bij de luchtvaartmaatschappij. De verdachte is een Omaans staatsburger. Hoe het kan dat hij wel in een toestel van Flydubai mocht vliegen, is nog onduidelijk. Hij werkt volgens de bronnen mee aan het onderzoek en zou inmiddels hebben toegegeven dat hij van plan was om het vliegtuig in Israël te laten neerstorten. clusters.headline: L'Inde et sa stratégie de corridors

items.title: L'Inde et sa stratégie de corridors
items.summary: En Inde, dès que l'on parle de sanctions contre la Russie ou bien l'Iran, c'est le transport qui en paye le prix. Fin septembre, le président américain Donald Trump a renforcé sa loi sur les tarifs douaniers contre la Russie. Ces sanctions s'adressent aussi à tous les pays qui commercent avec Moscou. Or, l'Inde, pénalisée par la guerre au Moyen-Orient et la fermeture du détroit d'Ormuz, a continué d'importer du pétrole russe. Dans ses derniers articles pour l'Institut de relations internationales et stratégiques (Iris), Olivier Da Lage, ancien journaliste à RFI et spécialiste de l'Inde, explique comment le pays cherche à bâtir de nouvelles routes pour diversifier son commerce.

items.title: Red scare: Solid GOP districts reeling from war, price backlash
items.summary: On Monday, as the war with Iran crossed the seven-month mark, Governor Greg Abbott declared a statewide disaster in Texas as a result of a massive increase in diesel prices and a deepening fuel shortage. Texas is hardly alone. Diesel prices have climbed nationwide since the war began, with the national average now around $6.45 per gallon , up from $3.76 when the war began in late February, according to data from AAA. A number of other states have recently taken steps to try to ease the costs of gas and diesel amid the ongoing war. As the midterm elections near and the war’s costs hit voters’ wallets, Abbott's declaration is a window into a larger problem for Republicans across the country, including some in deep red states. An increasing number of Republicans are being forced to spend money and political capital defending seats that they carried easily in recent elections. “The Iran War is proving to be a drag on Republicans, even in solidly Republican states,” Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former counsel to Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), told Responsible Statecraft in an email

items.title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine Malik
items.summary: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline UN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness. It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered an account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. clusters.headline: Hegseth says American forces have ‘destroyed’ Iran’s military

items.title: Hegseth says American forces have ‘destroyed’ Iran’s military
items.summary: Hegseth says American forces have ‘destroyed’ Iran’s military Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told a gathering of military leaders at Quantico Marine base on Wednesday that US forces have “destroyed” Iran’s navy, air force, defence systems, leadership and military-industrial capacity. Hegseth praised the American troops he addressed, crediting them with having destroyed Iran’s “entire defense space”. “Iran’s conventional shield has been crippled, and their nuclear ambitions have been crippled and laid bare for the world,” he added. Hegseth said the Pentagon has undergone a “clear break” from its past, with a “singular mission” of war-fighting. He said the department had fired “nearly 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force”, a figure he framed as “accountability” rather than a “purge”, as some media have called it. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth gives an address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, on 30 September 2026 (Alex Wong/AFP)

items.summary: Nato chief calls US war on Iran ‘absolutely essential’ Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said that it was “absolutely essential for the United States to take on Iran” in an interview at the Euronews Defence and Space summit on Wednesday. Only the US was “capable of taking out the nuclear capability of Iran”, Rutte said, describing the country's nuclear programme as a potential near-term threat “not only for Israel and the Middle East” but for Europe as well. While conceding that the Iran war had its “downsides”, he added that extra defence investments will enable European countries to “take care of their backyard themselves”. “It should be us taking care of the Houthis and the Red Sea”, rather than the US, Rutte said.

Under orders from President Calvin Coolidge, the U.S. Marines had intervened in Nicaragua to settle a civil war between a conservative government and liberal rebels. In his manifesto , Sandino responded by effectively declaring war on the United States. He also specifically denounced former liberal leaders who had agreed to put down their arms in the face of U.S. intervention. Speaking of General Moncada, the leading liberal officer who had agreed to end his revolt in talks convened by future Secretary of State Henry Stimson, Sandino wrote: “Nobody gave him the authority to abandon the ranks of the revolution to make secret agreements with the enemy.” One imagines there are Chavistas in Venezuela with similar feelings about interim President Delcy Rodriguez right now. clusters.headline: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?

items.title: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
items.summary: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues? For more than two decades, Iraq 's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York. The arrangement, created after the US -led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction. Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran 's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran. The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups. Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds. Read more: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?

items.title: Israel wants US-led force to disarm Lebanon's Hezbollah
items.summary: Fearing a security vacuum if UN peacekeepers leave southern Lebanon when their mandate expires December 31, the Lebanese government is desperately seeking an extension of the United Nations Interim Force (UNIFIL) or the creation of a European-led multinational force to take its place. Israel, which has occupied dozens of villages south of the Litani River since its latest invasion of the country earlier this year can't wait for the Blue Helmets to leave. It has long lobbied against UNIFIL’s extension, deeming it ineffective in taming and disarming Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militia. But Tel Aviv hasn't opposed an international force once UNIFIL leaves; it just doesn’t want one tied to the UN. Israel is lobbying for a U.S.-led force, while the Lebanese government prefers a European-led mission to aid the Lebanese army if UNIFIL’s mandate is not renewed or extended. An even bigger question is how exactly any such force can subdue battle-hardened Hezbollah, the country’s most powerful armed force. items.title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge
items.summary: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusade Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating. It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship. Continue reading...

A 22-year-old British male was arrested in London "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts", Britain's Counter-Terrorism Policing network said in a statement. Six men in their 20s have already been arrested and released on bail after three suspicious vans were stopped near the base in southwest England on September 27. items.summary: California leaders condemn Trump’s remarks about possible attacks on US cities California political leaders on Tuesday condemned President Donald Trump after he said Iran could “take out” US cities including Los Angeles and San Diego, describing the remarks as dangerous and unacceptable. Speaking at a political rally on Monday, Trump was discussing the economic costs of war when he said: “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego.” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said Trump’s remarks could compromise the city’s safety, while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said: “We are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” California Governor Gavin Newsom also criticised Trump, calling him “deranged”. Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president, adding that “no American city is expendable and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

items.title: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions'
items.summary: US and several allies say Iran committed 'terrorist actions' The US and nine other countries across the Americas in a joint statement condemned what they called Iran's "terrorist actions". The joint statement was released by the US and endorsed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago. "On 5 October, the undersigned nations, condemn the terrorist actions and other malign influence operations in our hemisphere by Iran and its terrorist proxies," it read. "These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security." The joint statement indicated that the countries "stand united" against "such threats", demanding that Tehran and "its proxies must halt these actions now".

items.title: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran
items.summary: Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran The chief executive of Saudi Aramco warned that the world's oil stockpiles are now "scarily thin". In his first public speech since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Amin Nasser said the conflict reduced oil supply from the region by "nearly 3bn barrels", with over 1bn barrels of oil released from reserves to cushion the depletion. Nasser estimated that "less than 6bn barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available". "The system is already straining," he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."

items.title: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis
items.summary: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could lead to a global food security crisis, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), John Denton, warned. According to the Wall Street Journal, Denton indicated that if the vital waterway is not reopened, grain prices could rise by up to 80 percent. The situation in the strait has also caused a shortage of around 2.7 million tons of fertiliser on the world market, a decrease of nearly 40 percent. Such obstacles could affect international agricultural production and food supplies, making import-dependent countries especially vulnerable. The report noted that the ICC is working with the UN and the International Maritime Organization on a mechanism that would transfer temporary management of navigation through the waterway to the UN secretary general. However, the ongoing tensions between the US and Iran have hindered its implementation, the report added.

items.title: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind
items.summary: On September 30, the U.S. completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq. Heralding this event, Iraq declared “Sovereignty Day,” celebrating the end of U.S. occupation and return of full sovereignty to the people of Iraq. In practice, this withdrawal was little more than the departure of a few hundred soldiers that had returned to Iraq in 2014 – at the invitation of the Iraqi government – to provide support and assistance to the collapsing Iraqi Army in its fight against ISIS. Unlike the hundreds of thousands of troops needed in Germany and Japan at the end of WWII, the troops of Operation Inherent Resolve were neither an occupation nor a challenge to sovereign control. Nonetheless, the mission had become a political liability and a convenient excuse for anti-government militias to maintain independence, retain weapons and force its will both in the streets and within Parliament. While some voices in Washington argue for a keeping residual military presence , the reasonable solution is shifting to a diplomatic and development effort. Instead, it would be stored at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, at least temporarily. items.title: Can Kurds in Iraq unite as US troops withdraw from the country?
items.summary: On September 21, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq officially announced the completion of the long-delayed unification and reorganization of its Peshmerga paramilitary forces under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs (MoPA). The Peshmerga are Kurdish armed forces, with roots going back to Kurdish guerrillas who fought as a more or less united front against successive Iraqi governments for most of the 20th century. After the 2003 invasion, though, they never came together as one Kurdish national army. Instead, they split into two separate party forces, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), each tied to one of the region's dominant political factions. Kurdish leaders hailed the September unification announcement as a historic victory for the Kurds in Iraq. Notably, the unification happened nine days before the final U.S. military withdrawal from Iraq. items.summary: De Verenigde Staten hebben alle twaalf bommenwerpers weggehaald van de Britse luchtmachtbasis Fairford. Dat zou zijn gebeurd vanwege een nieuwe dreiging die volgens Amerikaanse media afkomstig is van Iran. Vorige week werden er in de buurt van de basis in Fairford vijf Britse mannen aangehouden, die verdacht worden van het voorbereiden van een terroristische aanslag. Later werd nog een verdachte opgepakt. De Britse premier Burnham denkt net als de Amerikaanse president Trump dat Iran erachter zit. The New York Times schrijft dat er opnieuw dreigingen zijn binnengekomen. De krant spreekt van een "door Iran gesteund complot". Halsoverkop zouden de bommenwerpers zijn weggehaald. Een anonieme bron zegt tegen CNN dat het ongebruikelijk is dat bommenwerpers terug naar 'huis' worden gehaald, in plaats van dat ze naar een andere plek in de regio worden verplaatst. Basis gebruikt bij oorlog tegen Iran De bommenwerpers op de basis in Fairford werden door de Verenigde Staten gebruikt om Iran aan te vallen. items.title: Iranian oil minister steps down
items.summary: Iranian oil minister steps down Iran's oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, the president's office said in a statement on Sunday, amid long queues at petrol stations caused by the ongoing war and US sanctions. Government spokesperson Mehdi Tabatabaei told state TV later on Sunday that Paknejad, a member of President Pezeshkian's cabinet since August 2024, resigned for personal reasons "a long time ago." Hamid Bord, the CEO of the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), "has been appointed as acting Minister of Oil by a decree from the president", according to a statement carried by Iran’s state media. Bord has held senior positions at NIOC and previously headed several of its operating units, including the National Iranian South Oil Company and the Iranian Offshore Oil Company.

items.title: Iran airlines resume flights to Iraq’s Najaf after US exemption
items.summary: Iran airlines resume flights to Iraq’s Najaf after US exemption Iranian airlines resumed flights to Iraq ’s Najaf on Sunday after the United States granted Baghdad an exemption allowing sanctioned Iranian carriers to operate to the city holy to Shia Muslims, AFP reported. On Friday, the Iraqi government said it had secured an agreement with the US allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate 40 daily flights to and from Najaf. Last month, Iraq enforced the US ban on Iranian carriers, especially at Najaf’s airport, which is a major hub for Iranian flights. The US also granted Iraqi Airways, the national carrier, a waiver to fly between Najaf and Iran, with the flights expected to start this month.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi confirmed they had received a response via intermediaries to their proposal for a seven-day plan to reopen the contested Strait of Hormuz, which they presented at UN meetings in New York. He added that "the Islamic Republic of Iran’s final response is prepared [and] the necessary steps will be taken through the appropriate channels". US President Donald Trump said in late September that he had rejected the plan, but Iran has maintained that negotiations through mediators are ongoing. Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said earlier today that the strait will remain shut until Washington meets seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.

items.title: Iran says Hormuz Strait to remain closed until US meets seven conditions
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz Strait to remain closed until US meets seven conditions Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has said that the Strait of Hormuz will remain shut until Washington meets certain conditions. Ghalibaf, who also acts as Tehran's chief negotiator in the talks, said that the contested waterway will remain closed until seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding are met by Washington. He conceded that the US had made "some proposals through a mediator" after Tehran presented a seven-day roadmap to reopen the strait. But he warned Washington that "the era of wasting time and dictating unilateral demands is over" and Iran's position remains "clear and definite".

He told reporters that the return of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors has not been discussed by Iran's leadership. He noted that the peace process has been thwarted by the "volatility and fluctuation" of Washington's decision-making. “This is reflected in their conflicting statements as well as their fluctuating demands. items.title: Is China Trump's only hope for ending the Iran war?

At best, we are condemned to negotiations dominated by personal and political imperatives that seem to fit with a common description of insanity — to keep doing the same thing and expect a different result. At worst, the crisis raises the prospect that tactical nuclear weapons could be employed to solve it. items.summary: Three commercial vessels struck in Hormuz since 1 Oct, UKMTO says Attacks on commercial ships witnessed a surge during the past three days, as at least three tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) warnings. Early Saturday, UKMTO reported that a crude oil tanker was hit on its port side approximately 4 nautical miles east of Oman. A day earlier, an outbound vessel suffered a small fire and blackout, while a second crude tanker was struck nearby. On Thursday, a supertanker carrying 2.5 million barrels caught fire after being hit off Oman while transiting an unauthorised route, according to Iran's Fars news agency. In its weekly Voluntary Reporting Area Overview released on 2 October, UKMTO said 91 incidents of damage to vessels have been reported since February this year. Three tankers have been struck in and around the Strait of Hormuz since 1 October 2026. (AFP)

items.title: Iran's warns 'half-a-century-old' UAE over claim on three Gulf islands
items.summary: Iran's warns 'half-a-century-old' UAE over claim on three Gulf islands Ali Akbar Velayati, a senior adviser to Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, has warned the United Arab Emirates (UAE) against challenging Tehran and its sovereignty over three islands in the Persian Gulf. In a post on his X account, Velayati dismissed recent claims made by the UAE at the United Nations General Assembly regarding sovereignty over Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, and Abu Musa, saying the three islands will remain Iranian forever, according to IRNA. "A country whose political life does not reach half a century makes claims from the UN podium about islands that have been recorded under Iran's name in historical documents and maps of past centuries," Velayati said in the Farsi-language post. He added that the UAE should not "rely on foreign powers" for its security and should instead pursue good relations with its neighbours, IRNA reported. "The neighbour stays, and the guest goes… Regional experience has shown that imported security has an expiration date," said the former Iranian foreign minister.

items.summary: State Department says Iranian UN delegation duo expelled from US The United States has expelled two members of the Iranian delegation who attended the recent UN General Assembly after they ignored an order to leave the country, the State Department said Saturday. "Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in (New York) long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed. US media reported the State Department had told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation to leave the country Monday, and resorted to expelling the two members after learning from the Iranian mission to the UN they remained in the country on Friday. items.summary: Iranian rial at new low, as cenbank sells dollars to support currency Iran's rial continued its decline on Saturday, as the central bank announced an injection of up to $2 billion to support the currency while the economy faces US sanctions and a naval blockade. The US dollar was sold at around 2.688 million rials, up from 2.632 million on Friday, according to free-market tracking website bon-bast.com, while alanchand.com reported 2.695 million rials per dollar. State television said state banks began selling up to $2 billion to support the currency, which has lost more than half of its value in the past year. With an inflation rate of more than 70 percent, life is becoming ever tougher for ordinary citizens unable to afford basic necessities or rent ​as a US blockade cuts the state's financial lifeline – oil exports. Many Iranians seeking safe havens for their savings have been buying dollars, other hard currencies or gold.

items.title: L'Inde et sa stratégie de corridors

Or, l'Inde, pénalisée par la guerre au Moyen-Orient et la fermeture du détroit d'Ormuz, a continué d'importer du pétrole russe. Dans ses derniers articles pour l'Institut de relations internationales et stratégiques (Iris), Olivier Da Lage, ancien journaliste à RFI et spécialiste de l'Inde, explique comment le pays cherche à bâtir de nouvelles routes pour diversifier son commerce.

items.title: Red scare: Solid GOP districts reeling from war, price backlash
items.summary: On Monday, as the war with Iran crossed the seven-month mark, Governor Greg Abbott declared a statewide disaster in Texas as a result of a massive increase in diesel prices and a deepening fuel shortage. Texas is hardly alone. Diesel prices have climbed nationwide since the war began, with the national average now around $6.45 per gallon , up from $3.76 when the war began in late February, according to data from AAA. A number of other states have recently taken steps to try to ease the costs of gas and diesel amid the ongoing war. As the midterm elections near and the war’s costs hit voters’ wallets, Abbott's declaration is a window into a larger problem for Republicans across the country, including some in deep red states. An increasing number of Republicans are being forced to spend money and political capital defending seats that they carried easily in recent elections. “The Iran War is proving to be a drag on Republicans, even in solidly Republican states,” Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former counsel to Sen. items.title: Saudi-led coalition claims Houthis targeted power station in Medina
items.summary: Saudi-led coalition claims Houthis targeted power station in Medina The Saudi-led pro-government coalition in Yemen has claimed that the Houthi rebel group targeted a power centre in Medina in a drone attack on Tuesday, damaging one transformer but leaving the overall electricity network unaffected. Medina, in Saudi Arabia's western Hejaz region, is among the holiest cities in Islam. The Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, have seized territory in Yemen's southwest this month in a rapid offensive triggered by the Saudi bombing of Sanaa airport in July. The group has also bombed the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, through which Riyadh has diverted oil exports amid Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But the Houthis previously denied Saudi claims that they had targeted Mecca, the holiest place in Islam.

items.title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine Malik
items.summary: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline UN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness. It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered an account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Dat zei hij gisteravond in een interview bij de Amerikaanse nieuwszender Fox News. Hij voegde daar wel aan toe: "Maar het is geen geheim dat Iran Israëliërs in het buitenland wil aanvallen." Volgens Netanyahu wordt onderzocht of er banden zijn tussen Iran en de copiloot uit Oman die de gezagvoerder in de cockpit aanviel en waarschijnlijk als doel had het vliegtuig te laten crashen. Hegseth praised the American troops he addressed, crediting them with having destroyed Iran’s “entire defense space”. “Iran’s conventional shield has been crippled, and their nuclear ambitions have been crippled and laid bare for the world,” he added. He said the department had fired “nearly 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force”, a figure he framed as “accountability” rather than a “purge”, as some media have called it. items.title: UK PM says 'strong indications' Iran involved in airbase scare
items.summary: UK PM says 'strong indications' Iran involved in airbase scare British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident. "There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," Burnham told the BBC in an interview, referring to suspected bomb threat near the airbase in southwest England, which is used by the US military in its campaign against Tehran. Iran has denied involvement in the incident, and the five men arrested on suspicion of terrorist offences were later released on bail, with counterterrorism police saying that no improvised explosive devices were found in their vehicle, but a quantity of petrol was discovered.

items.title: Vance describes Iran’s leadership as ‘very confused’, says deal possible
items.summary: Vance describes Iran’s leadership as ‘very confused’, says deal possible US Vice President JD Vance said there is still scope for a deal with Iran if its leaders honour their commitments to Washington, while describing Tehran’s political decision-making system as “very confused”. In an interview with journalist Vince Coglianese, Vance said President Donald Trump had made clear that “there is a universe where we can strike a deal with Iran, but that requires the Iranians to behave”. He said Washington’s approach would be based on Iranian actions rather than statements. Vance said Iran’s leadership involved “a number of different constituencies”, including hardliners, conservatives, moderates and clerics. He also said Iran’s new supreme leader was “very detached” and not involved in day-to-day decision-making or public discussions about negotiations.

items.title: Lessons from the Iran War
items.summary: The Iran war offers broader lessons about the limits of force, the resilience of revolutionary regimes, and the unpredictability of modern conflict. Military action can weaken an adversary without producing decisive political outcomes, while economic pressure, alliances, energy markets, and public opinion can prove equally consequential. The conflict also exposed vulnerabilities in alliance coordination, munitions stocks, counter-drone capabilities, and strategic communication. Effective deterrence ultimately requires hard power, resilient partnerships, clear objectives, and the political will to sustain them.

First, the inflationary risks of throwing subsidies at the housing market at a moment when wider inflation, driven by energy prices and the Iran war, is on the march. Second, the political awkwardness of turning to George Osborne’s playbook. Third, the spectre of Jeff Fairburn, the shameless former boss of Persimmon who bagged a £75m bonus in 2018 as help to buy turbo-charged the value of his share-based incentives. items.summary: Iran supreme leader says US will be forced out of Middle East Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said on Monday that the United States would be forced to leave the Middle East after suffering "painful blows", according to a statement carried by state television. Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since the start of the war in late February, made the remarks despite attempts to revive talks aimed at ending the fighting. "Today, having suffered painful blows at the hands of valiant fighters and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they (the enemies) do not venture beyond the Arabian Sea," Khamenei said in the written statement attributed to him, without explicitly mentioning the United States. "Whenever they have braved this risk, they have only brought harm upon themselves. It will not be long before the Arabian Sea, too, would rid itself of their presence," he added.

items.title: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
items.summary: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues? For more than two decades, Iraq 's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York. The arrangement, created after the US -led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction. Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran 's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran. The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups. Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds. Read more: Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?

Data e luogo delle riprese non sono stati verificati in modo indipendente. items.title: Israel wants US-led force to disarm Lebanon's Hezbollah
items.summary: Fearing a security vacuum if UN peacekeepers leave southern Lebanon when their mandate expires December 31, the Lebanese government is desperately seeking an extension of the United Nations Interim Force (UNIFIL) or the creation of a European-led multinational force to take its place. Israel, which has occupied dozens of villages south of the Litani River since its latest invasion of the country earlier this year can't wait for the Blue Helmets to leave. It has long lobbied against UNIFIL’s extension, deeming it ineffective in taming and disarming Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militia. But Tel Aviv hasn't opposed an international force once UNIFIL leaves; it just doesn’t want one tied to the UN. Israel is lobbying for a U.S.-led force, while the Lebanese government prefers a European-led mission to aid the Lebanese army if UNIFIL’s mandate is not renewed or extended. An even bigger question is how exactly any such force can subdue battle-hardened Hezbollah, the country’s most powerful armed force. items.summary: RIYADH: The Yemeni Armed Forces have carried out 756 precision operations against Iran-backed Houthi military positions and capabilities across several fronts over the past 72 hours, the army’s official spokesman said on Sunday. Col. Majid Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said the operations targeted Houthi positions and personnel using aircraft, drones, missiles, field artillery and rocket launchers. items.title: Araghchi says Iran ready to resume war
items.summary: Araghchi says Iran ready to resume war Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said Iran is prepared for war to resume, “even if it comes to a doomsday war”. In an interview with NBC, Araghchi reiterated the terms of the country’s peace plan aimed at ending the war. "We want our assets, which are illegally frozen, be released. We want to be able to sell our oil. We want certain things that the US has already committed itself in the previous deals,” he said. This handout photograph shows Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaking at a meeting with diplomatic representatives from foreign countries in Tehran, on 16 June 2026 (Iranian foreign ministry/handout/AFP)

items.title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
items.summary: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’ The Trump administration ’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran ’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”. Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz. Continue reading...
